claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mentalizing task results, particularly the INT + PHYS condition.

claims.claim: The left IFG integrates the multiple constraints posed by the physical situation to set the ground for a correct reasoning process.
claims.source: The functional role of the left IFG in the context of tool use has been previously discussed (Reynaud et al., 2019) and a plausible hypothesis is that the left IFG integrates the multiple constraints posed by the physical situation to set the ground for a correct reasoning process, such as it could be involved in syntactic language processing (for a somewhat similar view, see Buxbaum and Randerath, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the role of the left IFG based on prior discussion and citations.

claims.claim: Language and tool use share syntactic processes in the basal ganglia of the brain.
claims.source: It has already been shown that language and tool use share syntactic processes in the basal ganglia of the brain (Thibault et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Thibault et al., 2021.

claims.claim: The activation of the LOTC might reflect the involvement of semantic processes.
claims.source: Thus, the activation of the LOTC might reflect the involvement of semantic processes whose involvement would remain to understand.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the LOTC activation.

claims.claim: The cortical thickness of the left area PF predicts technical-reasoning and visuospatial performance.
claims.source: A recent morphometry study (Federico et al., 2022) showed that the cortical thickness of the left area PF predicts technical-reasoning and visuospatial performance, whereas the right area PF only predicts visuospatial performance, confirming the distinction between these two abilities (Mitko and Fischer, 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Federico et al., 2022.

claims.claim: The cortical thickness of the right area PF only predicts visuospatial performance.
claims.source: A recent morphometry study (Federico et al., 2022) showed that the cortical thickness of the left area PF predicts technical-reasoning and visuospatial performance, whereas the right area PF only predicts visuospatial performance, confirming the distinction between these two abilities (Mitko and Fischer, 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Federico et al., 2022.

claims.claim: The right area PF is recruited along with the left area PF when the task makes high demands on both technical and visuospatial dimensions.
claims.source: These findings suggest that the right area PF is recruited along with the left area PF when the task makes high demands on both technical and visuospatial dimensions, as in the PHYS-Only condition of the mentalizing task.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the right area PF activation based on prior findings.

claims.claim: The left area PF is more involved in tasks that focus on the mechanical dimension of the tool-use action than its motor dimension.
claims.source: We have already shown that the left area PF is more involved in tasks that focus on the mechanical dimension of the tool-use action (e.g., the mechanical interaction between a tool and an object) than its motor dimension (i.e., the interaction between the tool and the effector [e.g., Reynaud et al., 2019; Reynaud et al., 2016]).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Reynaud et al., 2019 and Reynaud et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Recent accounts have proposed that non-social-cognitive skills such as causal understanding or technical reasoning might have played a crucial role in cumulative technological culture.
claims.source: Yet, recent accounts have proposed that non-social-cognitive skills such as causal understanding or technical reasoning might have played a crucial role in cumulative technological culture (Whiten, 2022; Osiurak et al., 2023; Vale et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Whiten, 2022, Osiurak et al., 2023, and Vale et al., 2021.

claims.claim: The improvement of technology over generations is accompanied by an increase in its understanding.
claims.source: Support for these accounts comes from micro-society experiments, which have demonstrated that the improvement of technology over generations is accompanied by an increase in its understanding (Osiurak et al., 2021; Osiurak et al., 2022), or that learners' technical-reasoning skills are a good predictor of cumulative performance in such micro-societies (De Oliveira et al., 2019; Osiurak et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Osiurak et al., 2021 and Osiurak et al., 2022.

claims.claim: Learners' technical-reasoning skills are a good predictor of cumulative performance in micro-societies.
claims.source: Support for these accounts comes from micro-society experiments, which have demonstrated that the improvement of technology over generations is accompanied by an increase in its understanding (Osiurak et al., 2021; Osiurak et al., 2022), or that learners' technical-reasoning skills are a good predictor of cumulative performance in such micro-societies (De Oliveira et al., 2019; Osiurak et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to De Oliveira et al., 2019 and Osiurak et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Fluid reasoning refers to temporarily maintaining information to produce adapted responses to solve novel problems or plan and execute directed behaviour based on inductive and deductive relationship.
claims.source: Fluid reasoning, hereafter called fluid cognition, refers to temporarily maintaining information to produce adapted responses to solve novel problems or plan and execute directed behaviour based on inductive and deductive relationship (Blair, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citation to Blair, 2006.

claims.claim: Fluid cognition does not necessitate knowledge of the physical world, its constraints and the mechanical laws governing it.
claims.source: Although fluid cognition is a non-verbal form of reasoning, it does not necessitate knowledge of the physical world, its constraints and the mechanical laws governing it.
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of fluid cognition that distinguishes it from technical reasoning.

claims.claim: The distinction between technical reasoning and fluid cognition has been supported by behavioural evidence.
claims.source: The distinction between technical reasoning and fluid cognition has already been supported by behavioural evidence (De Oliveira et al., 2019) as well as by neuroimaging studies that have shown the recruitment of the prefrontal cortex in fluid cognition (Hobeika et al., 2016), with brain regions that are not commonly reported in the context of tool use or physical understanding (e.g., dorsal prefrontal cortex and medial superior frontal gyrus).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to De Oliveira et al., 2019 and Hobeika et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Neuroimaging studies have shown the recruitment of the prefrontal cortex in fluid cognition.
claims.source: The distinction between technical reasoning and fluid cognition has already been supported by behavioural evidence (De Oliveira et al., 2019) as well as by neuroimaging studies that have shown the recruitment of the prefrontal cortex in fluid cognition (Hobeika et al., 2016), with brain regions that are not commonly reported in the context of tool use or physical understanding (e.g., dorsal prefrontal cortex and medial superior frontal gyrus).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hobeika et al., 2016.

claims.claim: The Raven's Progressive Matrices test has been widely used to predict performance on a wide range of logical reasoning tasks.
claims.source: This test has been widely used to predict performance on a wide range of logical reasoning tasks and has been found to predict the general factor of intelligence (Gray and Thompson, 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gray and Thompson, 2004.

claims.claim: The Raven's Progressive Matrices test has been found to predict the general factor of intelligence.
claims.source: This test has been widely used to predict performance on a wide range of logical reasoning tasks and has been found to predict the general factor of intelligence (Gray and Thompson, 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gray and Thompson, 2004.

claims.claim: Mentalizing refers to detecting and attributing mental states to others or oneself.
claims.source: Mentalizing refers to detecting and attributing mental states to others or oneself (Gallagher and Frith, 2003; Van Overwalle and Baetens, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citations to Gallagher and Frith, 2003 and Van Overwalle and Baetens, 2009.

claims.claim: Mentalizing is a form of causal reasoning.
claims.source: It is a form of causal reasoning, given that it can be used to infer how hidden mental states can cause some specific behaviours.
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of mentalizing based on its functional properties.

claims.claim: Mentalizing requires the collaboration of several cognitive mechanisms such as perspective taking (medial prefrontal cortex), the understanding of communicative gestures (temporoparietal junction including the angular gyrus) or knowledge about the person (temporal pole).
claims.source: Depending on the situation, this ability requires the collaboration of several cognitive mechanisms (Gallagher and Frith, 2003; Van Overwalle and Baetens, 2009), such as perspective taking (medial prefrontal cortex), the understanding of communicative gestures (temporoparietal junction including the angular gyrus) or knowledge about the person (temporal pole).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gallagher and Frith, 2003 and Van Overwalle and Baetens, 2009.

claims.claim: Mentalizing can require the indirect involvement of technical reasoning to apprehend the physical dimension of the situation.
claims.source: Frequently, this can also require the indirect involvement of technical reasoning to apprehend the physical dimension of the situation (e.g., it is raining, and two umbrellas can provide shelter from the rain), which can be crucial for inferring mental states (e.g., Alex uses one umbrella but does not give the other to Mary).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the interaction between mentalizing and technical reasoning.

claims.claim: All participants were right-handed, had a normal or corrected-to-normal vision, provided informed consent, and reported no history of neurological or psychiatric disorder.
claims.source: All the participants were right-handed, had a normal or corrected-to-normal vision, provided informed consent, and reported no history of neurological or psychiatric disorder.
claims.evidence: This is a direct report of participant inclusion criteria.

claims.claim: The study was in line with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by a French Ethics Committee (N°ID-RCB: 2018-A00734-51).
claims.source: The study was in line with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by a French Ethics Committee (N°ID-RCB: 2018-A00734-51).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about ethical approval.

claims.claim: In the mechanical problem-solving task, participants had to figure out how to move a red cube trapped in a 3D glass box from its original location to a new target location.
claims.source: In the scanner, the participants had to figure out for 4 s and for each mechanical problem how to solve it by using one of the tools shown before the scanning session.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental task as shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: In the psychotechnical task, participants had to select which of the two presented situations was the correct one or the most effective one.
claims.source: The participants had to select which of the two presented situations was the correct one or the most effective one in the experimental condition (Figure 1B), whereas, in the control condition, they had to select the situation containing a square (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental task as shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: In the fluid-cognition task experimental condition, participants were required to use fluid reasoning.
claims.source: The experimental condition required fluid reasoning (Figure 1C) whereas the control condition required only visuospatial pattern completion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental task as shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: In the mentalizing task PHYS-Only condition, the selection only needed to understand the physical context.
claims.source: In the PHYS-Only condition, the selection only needed to understand the physical context.
claims.evidence: This describes the PHYS-Only condition of the mentalizing task.

claims.claim: In the mentalizing task INT + PHYS condition, the selection needed to understand both the physical context and the social context.
claims.source: In the INT + PHYS condition, the selection needed to understand both the physical context and the social context.
claims.evidence: This describes the INT + PHYS condition of the mentalizing task.

claims.claim: A spherical ROI of the left area PF with a 5-mm radius was created in the MNI standard space (–59; –31; 40).
claims.source: Therefore, we created a spherical ROI of the left area PF with a 5-mm radius in the MNI standard space (–59; –31; 40).
claims.evidence: This is a direct description of the ROI analysis method.

claims.claim: The ROI was literature-defined to ensure the independence of its selection.
claims.source: This ROI was literature-defined to ensure the independence of its selection (Reynaud et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This explains the rationale for the ROI selection with citation to Reynaud et al., 2016.

claims.claim: The specific activation of the left area PF could not simply reflect that this area responds to a greater extent in a harder condition relative to an easy condition of a task.
claims.source: This interpretation is nevertheless ruled out by the results obtained with the fluid-cognition task.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the fluid-cognition task results that showed no activation despite being more difficult.

claims.claim: The findings invalidate the same-region-but-different-function interpretation.
claims.source: This finding invalidates the same-region-but-different-function interpretation by revealing a coherent pattern in the activation of the left area PF in situations in which participants were supposed to reason technically.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation analysis results.

claims.claim: The findings speak against the adjacency interpretation.
claims.source: These findings speak against the adjacency interpretation by revealing that participants recruited the same part of the left area PF to perform tasks involving technical reasoning.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spatial analysis of activation peaks.

claims.claim: Humans have created a wide range of technologies that have helped them colonize the whole surface of the Earth and beyond.
claims.source: Humans have created a wide range of technologies that have helped them colonize the whole surface of the Earth and beyond.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about human technological achievement supported by common knowledge.

claims.claim: The present study contributes to integrating cognitive science into the cultural evolution field.
claims.source: Following the effort undertaken by others (Bayani et al., 2021; Gärdenfors and Högberg, 2017; Gärdenfors, 2021; Strachan et al., 2021; Charbonneau et al., 2024; Sperber, 1996; Sperber and Hirschfeld, 2004), the present study contributes to integrating cognitive science into the cultural evolution field in which technical cognition – if not cognition (Heyes, 2016; Heyes, 2018) – has remained peripheral to the debate on the origins and evolution of human technology.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the contribution of the study supported by citations to related work.

claims.claim: Technical cognition has remained peripheral to the debate on the origins and evolution of human technology in the cultural evolution field.
claims.source: Following the effort undertaken by others (Bayani et al., 2021; Gärdenfors and Högberg, 2017; Gärdenfors, 2021; Strachan et al., 2021; Charbonneau et al., 2024; Sperber, 1996; Sperber and Hirschfeld, 2004), the present study contributes to integrating cognitive science into the cultural evolution field in which technical cognition – if not cognition (Heyes, 2016; Heyes, 2018) – has remained peripheral to the debate on the origins and evolution of human technology.
claims.evidence: This claim characterizes the state of the field and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: Archaeologists have tended to privilege language and symbol use in discussion of the modern mind.
claims.source: As Wynn et al., 2017 stated, '[e]ven archaeologists, for whom technical remains are the primary data source, have tended to privilege language and symbol use in discussion of the modern mind' (p. 21).
claims.evidence: This is a direct quote from Wynn et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The present findings offer a neural reality to behavioural results on technical reasoning and cumulative technological culture.
claims.source: While behavioural experiments tend to demonstrate the impact of technical reasoning on cumulative technological culture, the present findings offer a neural reality to these behavioural results and inspire new questions: Which, if any, cognitive subcomponents of technical reasoning are specific to the human species?
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the contribution of the present study's findings.

results.result: Two fMRI experiments were conducted with 34 participants in Experiment 1 and 35 participants in Experiment 2. All participants met inclusion criteria (right-handed, normal vision, no neurological/psychiatric history) and the study received ethical approval.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C35 and C85-C86 provide clear methodological details about participant recruitment, sample sizes, inclusion criteria, and ethical approval. These are straightforward descriptive claims that are well-documented in the methods section.

results.result: Experimental conditions were significantly more difficult than control conditions across all tasks (p < 0.05), with some participants performing at or below chance level in experimental but not control conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C38 report behavioral validation showing experimental conditions were harder than controls with statistical support (p < 0.05). This establishes that the experimental manipulations successfully created differential task difficulty, which is important for interpreting the neuroimaging results.

results.result: The left area PF within the supramarginal gyrus is systematically recruited across all tasks requiring physical understanding, including mechanical problem-solving, psychotechnical reasoning, and both conditions of the mentalizing task. Conjunction analysis confirmed that only the left area PF was commonly activated across all four experimental conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C42 and C59 are strongly supported by whole-brain fMRI analyses showing consistent left area PF activation across multiple tasks involving physical reasoning. The conjunction analysis (C41) provides particularly strong evidence by identifying the left area PF as the only region commonly activated across all conditions. This supports the generalizability hypothesis.

results.result: The technical-reasoning network, particularly the left area PF, is not recruited during fluid cognition tasks. The fluid-cognition task instead activated dorsal prefrontal and medial superior frontal cortices, with no activation in inferior parietal lobes. ROI analysis confirmed no significant activation of left area PF (p = 0.35).
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C44, C53, and C60-C62 demonstrate specificity of the technical-reasoning network by showing it is not engaged during non-physical reasoning. The whole-brain analysis, ROI analysis, and control for task difficulty (participants performing below 50% removed) all converge to support this dissociation between technical reasoning and fluid cognition.

results.result: The mentalizing task revealed that technical reasoning (left area PF) and mentalizing networks are distinct but can interact. The INT+PHYS condition activated both networks, while the contrast INT+PHYS > PHYS-Only isolated the mentalizing network (temporoparietal junctions, medial prefrontal cortex, temporal pole) without technical-reasoning areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 and C63-C64 are supported by careful contrast analyses showing that mentalizing and technical reasoning recruit distinct networks that can work together. The contrast analysis (C47-C48) is particularly important as it isolates the mentalizing-specific activation, demonstrating that the two forms of causal reasoning are neurally dissociable.

results.result: ROI analyses confirmed greater activation of the left area PF in mechanical problem-solving, psychotechnical, and both mentalizing conditions (all p < 0.001), but not in fluid cognition (p = 0.35).
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C53 provide convergent ROI-based evidence supporting the whole-brain findings. The use of a literature-defined ROI (C92-C93) ensures independence. The statistical significance is clearly reported with appropriate p-values, and the pattern matches the whole-brain results.

results.result: Correlational analyses revealed significant correlations between all technical reasoning tasks (psychotechnical, PHYS-Only, INT+PHYS; all p < 0.05) but no correlations with fluid cognition (all p > 0.15), invalidating the same-region-but-different-function interpretation.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 and C95 provide important evidence that the left area PF activation reflects a coherent cognitive process across technical reasoning tasks. The correlation analysis addresses a key alternative interpretation and strengthens the claim that this region supports a unified technical reasoning function rather than multiple unrelated processes.

results.result: Spatial analysis of individual activation peaks showed that technical reasoning tasks recruited the same posterior part of left area PF (y coordinates not significantly different, all p > 0.05), while fluid cognition peaks were more anterior in area PFt and postcentral cortex (all p < 0.05 vs. technical reasoning tasks).
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 and C96 address the adjacency interpretation through careful spatial analysis of individual peaks. The statistical comparison of y-coordinates provides quantitative evidence that technical reasoning tasks recruit the same anatomical location, while fluid cognition activates a distinct anterior region. This strengthens the specificity claim.

results.result: The specific activation of left area PF in technical reasoning tasks cannot be explained by task difficulty alone, as demonstrated by the fluid-cognition task showing no activation despite being more difficult than its control condition.
results.evaluation: Claim C94 addresses an important confound by showing that difficulty alone does not drive left area PF activation. The fluid-cognition task provides a critical control: it was harder than its baseline but showed no left area PF activation, ruling out a general difficulty explanation. Additional analyses removing low-performing participants further support this conclusion.

results.result: A technical-reasoning process is specifically at work in physical problem-solving situations, with the left area PF being central to this process in both tool-use and non-tool-use contexts. This demonstrates the existence of a specific cognitive module dedicated to materiality.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C8 represent the main conclusions of the study and are well-supported by the convergent evidence from multiple tasks, whole-brain analyses, ROI analyses, correlation analyses, and spatial analyses. The claim of a 'specific cognitive module' (C8) is justified by the consistent activation pattern and functional specificity demonstrated across analyses.

results.result: The cognitive module for technical reasoning might support the accumulation of technical knowledge over generations and cumulative technological culture. The present findings provide neural evidence for behavioral results linking technical reasoning to cumulative technological culture.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C72-C74, C98, and C101 make broader theoretical claims about the role of technical reasoning in cultural evolution. While C72-C74 cite behavioral evidence from other studies, the present neuroimaging data do not directly test cumulative culture or knowledge transmission. The claim that the left area PF 'might be' the supporting pillar (C9) is appropriately hedged but remains speculative without longitudinal or developmental data.

results.result: The left IFG may integrate multiple constraints in physical situations to support technical reasoning, potentially sharing syntactic processes with language. The LOTC activation might reflect semantic processing of familiar tools and objects.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 offer speculative interpretations of additional brain regions in the technical-reasoning network. While C66 cites evidence for shared syntactic processes in basal ganglia, the functional roles proposed for IFG (C65) and LOTC (C67) are explicitly marked as hypotheses requiring further investigation. These interpretations go beyond what the current data directly demonstrate.

results.result: The cortical thickness of left area PF predicts technical-reasoning and visuospatial performance, while right area PF only predicts visuospatial performance. The right area PF may be recruited when tasks make high demands on both technical and visuospatial dimensions.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C69 cite prior morphometry work (Federico et al., 2022) but are not directly tested in this study. Claim C70's interpretation of right area PF recruitment is speculative and the authors themselves note it is 'unlikely' given that other tasks should also show this pattern. This interpretation requires additional evidence.

results.result: Human materiality (using, making, creating, and passing on technologies) has enabled humans to shape the physical world. Scientists have focused on low-level or high-level skills to explain this, with little attention to intermediate-level technical cognition.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4, C10-C14, and C97 provide background context and motivation for the study. These are general statements about human technology and the state of the field, supported by citations and common knowledge. They appropriately frame the research question but are not primary findings of this study.

results.result: Prior neuropsychological and neuroimaging research has established that damage to the left inferior parietal lobe (particularly area PF) impairs tool use, and that this region is activated during tool observation and physical reasoning. However, the manipulation-based approach has limitations in explaining broader aspects of human technology.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C27 accurately summarize prior literature on the neural basis of tool use and technical cognition. These claims are well-supported by appropriate citations and provide essential context for the current study. They establish the foundation for the technical-reasoning hypothesis being tested.

results.result: Technical reasoning is defined as the ability to reason about physical properties of objects, nurtured by implicit mechanical knowledge. It is both causal and analogical, uses prior knowledge about mechanical properties and physical laws, and produces simulations of mechanical actions. The left area PF is central to this network.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C33 define the technical-reasoning hypothesis that the study tests. These definitional and theoretical claims are clearly stated and provide the conceptual framework for interpreting the empirical findings. They are appropriately characterized as knowledge-based claims that guide the experimental design.

results.result: Fluid cognition refers to maintaining information to solve novel problems through inductive and deductive reasoning, does not require knowledge of the physical world, and is supported by prefrontal cortex activation. It is behaviorally and neurally distinct from technical reasoning.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C80 define fluid cognition and cite prior evidence for its neural basis and distinction from technical reasoning. These claims appropriately establish the theoretical basis for using fluid cognition as a control condition to test the specificity of technical reasoning.

results.result: Mentalizing is a form of causal reasoning involving detection and attribution of mental states, requiring collaboration of multiple cognitive mechanisms. It can require indirect involvement of technical reasoning to understand physical dimensions of social situations.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C84 define mentalizing and its neural basis, supported by appropriate citations. Claim C84's proposal that mentalizing can involve technical reasoning is a theoretical claim that the study tests empirically through the mentalizing task design. These claims provide the rationale for examining interactions between social and physical reasoning.

results.result: The study employed four distinct tasks: mechanical problem-solving (novel tool use), psychotechnical (non-tool physical reasoning), fluid cognition (Raven's matrices adaptation), and mentalizing (with PHYS-Only and INT+PHYS conditions). ROI analysis used a literature-defined spherical ROI of left area PF.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C93 describe the experimental tasks and ROI methodology. These are clearly documented methodological details that are essential for interpreting and replicating the results. The use of a literature-defined ROI (C93) is appropriate for ensuring independence of the ROI selection.

results.result: Prior work has shown the left area PF is more involved in mechanical than motor dimensions of tool use. Technical cognition has remained peripheral to debates on human technological evolution, with archaeologists tending to privilege language and symbol use.
results.evaluation: Claims C71, C99-C100 cite prior research and characterize the state of the field. These claims are appropriately supported by citations and provide context for the study's contribution. They help establish why investigating technical cognition is important for understanding human evolution.

results.result: The left area PF within the left parietal lobe is central for technical reasoning across multiple physical problem-solving tasks. This was demonstrated through whole-brain fMRI analyses showing consistent activation of left area PF in the mechanical problem-solving task, psychotechnical task, and both conditions of the mentalizing task (PHYS-Only and INT+PHYS), confirmed by ROI analyses (all p < 0.001). A conjunction analysis across all four experimental conditions revealed activation only in the left supramarginal gyrus including left area PF.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirmed this as a key finding, with the editor noting 'solid evidence was shown regarding the commonalities and differences across different types of reasoning tasks.' One reviewer stated the study 'offers valuable insights into the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying technical reasoning' and acknowledged that 'additional analyses have enhanced the reliability of the findings.' The consistent activation pattern across tasks was accepted as demonstrating the central role of left area PF.

results.result: The technical-reasoning network is not recruited during fluid cognition tasks, demonstrating specificity of technical reasoning to the physical domain. The fluid-cognition task activated dorsal prefrontal cortices and medial superior frontal cortices but showed no activation of inferior parietal lobes. ROI analysis confirmed no greater activation of left area PF in the fluid-cognition task (p = 0.35), distinguishing technical reasoning from other forms of non-verbal causal reasoning.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this finding as demonstrating specificity. One reviewer noted the study 'demonstrate[s] the specificity of technical reasoning, finding that area PF is not involved in the fluid-cognition task.' The editor confirmed 'solid evidence was shown regarding the commonalities and differences across different types of reasoning tasks.' This negative result was validated through ROI analysis as requested by reviewers.

results.result: Technical reasoning and mentalizing networks can interact to solve problems combining social and physical constraints. The INT+PHYS condition activated both left area PF (technical reasoning) and bilateral mentalizing areas (temporoparietal junctions, medial prefrontal cortices, temporal pole). The contrast INT+PHYS > PHYS-Only isolated the mentalizing network without technical-reasoning areas, showing distinct but interacting networks for different domains of causal reasoning.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this finding without challenge. One reviewer acknowledged the study shows 'area PF is central to technical reasoning and plays an essential role in tool-use and non-tool-use physical problem-solving, as well as both conditions of mentalizing tasks.' The demonstration of network interaction was treated as a valid contribution showing how distinct reasoning systems can work together.

results.result: Correlation analysis revealed significant correlations between all technical reasoning tasks (psychotechnical, PHYS-Only, INT+PHYS; all p < 0.05) but no correlation with the fluid-cognition task (all p > 0.15). This pattern invalidates the 'same-region-but-different-function' interpretation by showing coherent activation patterns across technical reasoning situations.
results.evaluation: One reviewer raised concerns that correlation analysis 'does not rule out the so-called same region different function interpretation because it relies on correlation—one cannot reverse infer that the left SMG is carrying out the same function across different tasks because the response in that area is more strongly correlated between certain tasks.' The reviewer noted this 'points to that possibility and makes interesting predictions for future studies' but cannot definitively establish common function. Another reviewer noted limitations due to different subject samples and scanning runs.

results.result: Spatial analysis of activation peaks showed that technical reasoning tasks recruited the same posterior region (left area PF) while fluid cognition activated more anterior regions (left area PFt and postcentral cortex). The y coordinates of technical reasoning task peaks were significantly more posterior than fluid cognition peaks (all p < 0.05), with no differences among the four technical reasoning tasks (all p > 0.05), speaking against the adjacency interpretation.
results.evaluation: One reviewer questioned the analysis approach, asking 'why restrict the analysis to just the Y coordinate?' and suggested 'a rigorous way to test the adjacency hypothesis is to compute Euclidean distance among X, Y, and Z coordinates between any two tasks.' The reviewer stated 'there is no justification to restrict this analysis to the anterior-posterior dimension only,' indicating the evidence is incomplete for fully addressing the adjacency interpretation.

results.result: Behavioral results showed that experimental conditions were significantly more difficult than control conditions across all tasks (all p < 0.05), with some participants performing at or below chance level in experimental but not control conditions. This difficulty difference was interpreted as validating the experimental manipulation.
results.evaluation: Multiple reviewers expressed persistent concerns about differential task difficulty. One reviewer noted 'the concern remains that area PF was driven harder by the experimental task in part due to the more challenging nature of that task' and that the authors' response 'seems to sidestep the central point.' Another reviewer identified 'a major limitation' that 'participants made a button press response only to the last trial in a block,' making it 'not possible for one to know if participants who are at chance are performing differently from participants who are not at chance.' The removal of below-50% performers was deemed 'somewhat helpful' but insufficient.

results.result: The results demonstrate the existence of a specific cognitive module in the human brain dedicated to materiality, which might be the supporting pillar allowing the accumulation of technical knowledge over generations. This conclusion is drawn from consistent activation of left area PF across physical reasoning tasks.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the core finding of a dedicated neural system for technical reasoning. The editor described it as a 'valuable study' that 'will make a useful contribution to our understanding of some of the computations performed by area PF.' One reviewer stated the work 'enhances our understanding of the neurocognitive basis of technical reasoning that supports advanced technologies.' The speculative aspect about cultural transmission was not challenged.

results.result: The technical-reasoning network includes left area PF as central, along with additional brain areas such as left IFG and LOTC. The left IFG may integrate multiple constraints from physical situations, while LOTC activation might reflect semantic processes, though these interpretations remain speculative.
results.evaluation: One reviewer raised a fundamental concern about the interpretation: 'The discussion of the left SMG in the manuscript is prominent and narrowly construed—the left SMG is discussed as if it were 'the' region.' The reviewer noted that 'if one were to relax the threshold...there will be overlapping voxels outside the SMG' and asked 'is there a counterfactual or alternative brain area/network/system not in the left SMG?' This suggests the network characterization may be incomplete or overly focused on one region.

results.result: The specific activation of left area PF in technical reasoning tasks cannot simply reflect greater difficulty, as ruled out by the fluid-cognition task results which showed no PF activation despite being more difficult than its control condition.
results.evaluation: One reviewer explicitly challenged this interpretation, stating 'this response seems to sidestep the central point of the reviewers' concerns: the fundamental computations that underlie the technical reasoning tasks may also be present in the respective (non technical-reasoning-based) control tasks and drive area PF activations to greater or lesser degrees based on how much they tax those computations.' The reviewer noted that the fluid cognition comparison 'does not mitigate this concern, it just suggests that neither of those tasks tap the same fundamental computations.'

comparisons.comparison: Both address behavioral validation (C36-C38) showing experimental conditions were harder than controls. OpenEval rated this as SUPPORTED, finding the statistical evidence adequate. Peer reviewers rated it UNCERTAIN, expressing persistent concerns that differential difficulty confounds interpretation of neural results and that the response methodology (button press only on last trial) prevents proper assessment of participant performance.

Both evaluate specificity claims (C43-C44, C53, C60-C62) showing left area PF is not engaged during non-physical reasoning. Both rated this SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasized convergent evidence from whole-brain and ROI analyses. Peer reviewers confirmed 'solid evidence' for differences across reasoning types and accepted the negative result for fluid cognition.

Both address correlation analysis (C54-C55, C95) testing whether left area PF reflects coherent cognitive process. OpenEval rated SUPPORTED, viewing correlation as evidence for unified function. Peer reviewers rated UNCERTAIN, noting correlation 'does not rule out the so-called same region different function interpretation' and that one cannot reverse infer common function from correlation alone.

Both evaluate spatial analysis of peak coordinates (C56-C58, C96) addressing adjacency interpretation. OpenEval rated SUPPORTED, finding y-coordinate comparison provides quantitative evidence for same anatomical location. Peer reviewers rated UNCERTAIN, questioning why analysis was restricted to y-coordinate only and suggesting Euclidean distance across all coordinates would be more rigorous.

Both address claim C94 about difficulty confound. OpenEval rated SUPPORTED, viewing fluid cognition as adequate control showing difficulty alone doesn't drive activation. Peer reviewers rated UNCERTAIN, arguing the response 'sidesteps the central point' that fundamental computations may drive area PF to varying degrees, and fluid cognition comparison only shows those tasks don't tap the same computations.

Both evaluate dissociation between mentalizing and technical reasoning networks (C46-C48, C63-C64, plus C7 in peer review). Both rated SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasized contrast analysis isolating mentalizing-specific activation. Peer reviewers accepted the finding that distinct networks can work together, with one reviewer acknowledging area PF's role across both mentalizing conditions.

Both address core finding of consistent left area PF activation across technical reasoning tasks (C39-C42, C59, plus C5-C6, C49-C52 in peer review). Both rated SUPPORTED. OpenEval highlighted conjunction analysis as particularly strong evidence. Peer reviewers affirmed 'solid evidence' and 'valuable insights,' with editor noting enhanced reliability from additional analyses.
